# 19-veles — sources

Back-test entry `19-veles.yaml`: Veles, a pricing copilot for enterprise sales teams (YC Winter 2024, W24).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's choice"
marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC post of
2024-02-23 and the months around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one exists;
anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Veles - Your copilot for enterprise sales", 2024-02-23 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/KTD-veles-your-copilot-for-enterprise-sales
- [HOME24] getveles.com as archived 2024-04-19 (home page with customer quotes) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240419015813/https://www.getveles.com/
- [PRICE24] getveles.com/pricing as archived 2024-05-25, the first archived snapshot of the pricing page (the next, 2024-06-17, is identical) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240525193905/https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [PRICE] getveles.com/pricing today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [YCP] YC company page today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/veles
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/sales/wholesale-and-manufacturing-sales-representatives.htm

No Launch HN exists (HN search for Veles finds no launch thread: https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?query=Veles&tags=story).

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Account executives who price and quote enterprise software deals; their sales leadership.
   [LYC] "equip your sales team with an AI-powered quoting tool ... give reps a tool they will actually love, and
   leadership the actionable insights they need to move the needle." [LYC] "we're on a mission to make every rep a top
   performer." → `roles[rep]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "selling software to enterprises" (the
   post's "SaaS Pricing Calculator" and "enterprise sales deals").

2. **What (the job).** Price each enterprise deal accurately and on standard terms.
   [LYC] "Pricing enterprise sales deals is a headache. Fragmented processes and tools result in subpar terms and lost
   opportunities." [LYC] the solution ensures "accurate pricing and standard terms". → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When a buyer asks for a quote and the pricing has to be worked out and approved.
   [LYC] "Many teams resort to complex Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains just to handle
   pricing." [LYC] the tool helps reps "navigate the quoting and negotiation process effectively". [HOME24] (a customer)
   "Veles gives us those insights while optimizing a daily activity for salespeople and saving them time."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: deal quote`. Author's choice: the window {4, WEEKS} (a weekly rhythm, the
   diversity research's reading; spec 120's WEEKS) and Frequency 2 to 4 weeks out of 4. Prevalence `p_80_100`: an
   account executive on an enterprise team quotes at least once in four weeks.

4. **Which people.** Sales teams of up to ten at US software companies selling enterprise deals.
   [PRICE24] both paid plans are "Up to 10 team members". [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI
   platforms". → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (the team and the testimonials are US; no other
   market is named).

5. **Who pays.** The sales team's budget; the sales director chooses; finance agrees to the discount rules.
   [LYC] "Leadership lacks scalable insight into sales negotiations, hindering optimization and guidance for sales
   reps." [HOME24] the quoted customers are a "Founder & CEO", a "President & Cofounder" and a "VP of Business
   Development". → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`, Buyer and payer tests "The CFO" (a RevOps lead listed).
   Author's choice: no source names the buyer's title or who must agree; the CFO is the author's reading of "deal desk
   rules" and "minimize discounting" (discount policy is finance's). Purchase friction's three items (a CRM check —
   tested; agreeing the discount rules with finance; a security review) are the author's, the first from [LYC]
   "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI platforms" and [PRICE24] "Pre-built Integrations" on Growth.
   Commitment's step, "try it on one sales team's deals": [LYC] "Book a demo with us here"; the trial is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** One calculator with the price book, the deal desk rules and peer benchmarks; leadership sees every
   deal's pricing.
   [LYC] "Veles offers an easy-to-use calculator, benchmarks for comparing deals against those of peers, and clear
   guidance on deal desk rules, ensuring accurate pricing and standard terms." [LYC] "SaaS Pricing Calculator: Easily
   standardize pricing and track sales rep behavior in one intuitive platform." [LYC] "designed to enhance negotiation
   skills, minimize discounting, and land larger deals with confidence." [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are
   negotiating, discounting, offering concessions, and presenting pricing to your customers."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (the deal already in the CRM — tested; a written price
   book; one tool) and Adoption friction (every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets — tested; record each
   concession). Relative advantage's two benefits: [HOME24] (a customer) "a well engineered pricing calculator provided
   reps to close deals faster" (shorter_time) and [LYC] "minimize discounting" (fewer_attempts, fewer rounds of
   discount); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $250 to $500 per sales team a month; the cost is deals lost or signed on worse terms.
   [PRICE24] "Startup ... $250.00 USD /month ... Up to 10 team members"; "Growth ... $500.00 USD /month ... Pre-built
   Integrations ... Up to 10 team members"; "Enterprise ... Contact Sales". → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $250 to
   $500 per sales team (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 2 to 4 deals of the deals they quote per sales team a month, lossPhrase "Deals lost or
   signed on worse terms because the pricing was worked out by hand": author's reading of [LYC] "subpar terms and lost
   opportunities"; no source gives a count or a percent. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a count of
   deals never compares with dollars). `hourly_rate` 50 (the loader wants one on a B2B entry; the chain does not read
   it): [BLS] "$104,920 in May 2025" for technical and scientific products, about $50 an hour.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "Slow Ramp: Onboarding new sales reps takes 5 - 7 months due to poorly documented pricing strategies and
   variations across companies." [LYC] "No Knowledge Share: Top performers' insights are trapped, preventing learning
   and team-wide improvement." [HOME24] "There is also a lot of information that is lost in the front end of the
   negotiation." [YCP] (today, a later framing used only for one story) "You closed your first few deals on handshakes
   and Stripe links. Now a customer wants a ramp-up, custom terms, or annual billing — and suddenly you're duct-taping
   spreadsheets to your CRM."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Account executives (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Jordan Okafor → [LYC] "Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains"; the ramp and the two-day approval wait are the author's.
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [LYC] the slow ramp and "poorly documented pricing strategies"; a new rep asking three people.
- Mateo Fernández → author's invention, filling a gap: a rep whose CPQ already holds the price book, so the problem is not a chorus; against on Importance.
- Aisha Bello → [LYC] "minimize discounting"; [HOME24] "information that is lost in the front end of the negotiation": a discount given without knowing what similar deals closed at.
- Connor Walsh → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Tobias Becker → author's invention: a gate No (on leave in the window).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → author's invention: a gate No (only renewals, quoted by another team, in the window).
- Darnell Hayes → [YCP]'s later "handshakes and Stripe links" framing: a small seller whose deals are not in a CRM, so the tested condition fails (Compatibility only with help).
- Ingrid Halvorsen → [LYC] "Top performers' insights are trapped": a top performer who trusts her own sheet (Current solution mostly works; Relative advantage negative).
- Rahul Menon → [LYC] "email chains"; the deal desk approval and three versions of one quote are the author's.
- Sofia Marchetti → [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are negotiating, discounting, offering concessions": logging every concession is more admin (Adoption friction probably not).

Sales directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Grant Whitaker, Tanya Brooks → [HOME24] the customers' praise ("gives us insights we haven't had before"): pay within the plans, the CFO agrees.
- Kwabena Asante → [PRICE24] "Enterprise ... Contact Sales": a larger team that would pay above $500 (beyond the founder's band).
- Lucia Moreno, Elena Petrova → [LYC] "Book a demo"; [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ": would start only after a demo or a live-deal trial.
- Heather Lindqvist → author's invention: a small team that would pay under $250 until it is proven.
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention, filling a gap: a team whose CPQ already quotes; Nothing as the cost, would not pay.
- Victor Nakamura → author's invention: the price set against what the CRM costs; someone else agreed.

The share at or above $250 (5 of 8) is the author's: no public account gives Veles's conversion at launch; the
customer quotes on [HOME24] are vendor-curated. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder.

## Status today

Widened. [YCP] now reads "CPQ for humans and agents" and addresses early-stage founders ("Veles is built for you. AI
agents handle quoting, approvals, and deal docs end-to-end so you can run a real sales motion without hiring a deal
desk."). Price today, [PRICE]: "Pay per active contract, not per seat"; "$ 8 / contract / mo First 10 contracts free.
Unlimited seats. No credit card required to start."; Enterprise "Custom". The launch-era per-team plans ($250 and $500 a
month) are gone.

## Could not be sourced

- **The cost.** The launch post names the loss ("subpar terms and lost opportunities") but no number; the 2 to 4 deals
  per sales team a month is the author's reading in the founder's terms, chosen as a count a sales director can recall.
- **The price at launch itself.** The first archived pricing page is three months after the Launch YC post; it is
  used as the launch-era price (no earlier price is public).
- **The buyer's title and who must agree.** No source names them; "Sales directors" and "The CFO" are the author's.
- **A launch-era rate of how often a rep quotes.** The weekly rhythm is the diversity research's reading; [LYC] says
  only that pricing is handled per deal.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person rep accounts.** None exists; the occasions are scripted from [LYC], [HOME24]
  (vendor-curated quotes) and one later framing from [YCP].
- The launch post's quota line ("On average 60% of sales reps hit quota due to fragmented tooling") reads as if
  "miss" was meant; it is not used as a figure.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction items, the Purchase friction items but the CRM check, and every pick are the
  author's.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to sending, but the recency screen (4) sits between two context screens that carry the same headline (3 and 5), so the context step feels split in two around it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 both ask 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.' It reads as the same context question asked twice.
founder.missing: Nothing about my solution or price. The flow never asks for the calculator with the price book, deal desk rules and peer benchmarks, or my $250 to $500 per sales team a month. It also never asks what the problem costs (deals lost or signed on worse terms) or who pays: the sales director chooses and finance has to agree to the discount rules. And it never asks about the second audience, sales leadership, who want to see how every deal was priced.

PRIMARY.order_why: Asking which part I'd most like made easier before asking how my last quote actually went feels backwards, since recalling the last quote first would ground my pick.
PRIMARY.missing: How long the approval took and who had to sign off (the two-day wait for discount approval is the slowest part for me), and where I find pricing guidance or discount rules when they aren't written down.

screens.instead: How should account executives answer? — Daphne asks aloud on video (ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap (ready now) / Let them pick when they open the link (ready when Daphne is)

screens.why1: After choosing how account executives answer, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words a sales founder reads at once; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own page but its description makes it clear.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching AEs I know by name from my network and our design partners, so it's answerable from my own work.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list, and an open group link are distinct and cover how I'd reach AEs; no option is missing for me.
screens.why5: Nothing here drifts from what I typed and nothing of Veles leaks to the account executives.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside a number, but the line names only Frequency even though Importance and Current solution are just as short, and it leaves out the '5 needed' that would make the call clear.
screens.why_b2: The tally and the bars are plain, but I need a second look to work out why only 4 of my 7 respondents count on three cards when 6 of 7 said yes on Prevalence.
screens.why_b3: The Importance and Current solution lines are word for word what I checked, and Prevalence and Frequency are my quote-and-approval occasion over four weeks, so I recognise all of them.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' hints that I need more answers, but the screen never tells me to send the study to more account executives or how many more.
screens.why_b5: Prevalence is called 'Holding up' at exactly the bar on only 7 people with no low-n caution, and the drop from 7 answered to 4 counted is not explained.
screens.instead: Too few to call on 3 of 4 beliefs: only 4 of 7 reached Frequency, Importance and Current solution (5 needed each), so send the study to a few more account executives; Prevalence holds, just, at 6 of 7.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I see both the result and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip runs 0 to 7 with six cells for me, one against and the marker at 6, so what is counted, over how many and where my bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: I described the moment as a buyer asking for a quote that has to be worked out and approved, and 'got approval for an enterprise deal quote' is recognisably that, but narrower: a rep still waiting on approval would answer no.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' plus a pointer to the next two cards tells me where to look, not what this means for Veles, such as whether quoting is frequent enough to sell a per-team plan.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and 'at your bar exactly' does not dress 6 of 7 up as strong.
screens.instead: Ask whether they worked out a quote for a buyer in the last 4 weeks, not whether it was approved, and say that 6 of 7 clearing an 8-in-10 bar means the moment is common enough to build on, while one more no would have dropped it below.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits beside "5 needed to call it", but the number under it says "4 answered" when six answered and four were counted, so the deciding figure is mislabelled beside the verdict.
screens.why_b2: The axis plainly counts weeks out of 4 with the middle answer at 3, but the bar reads "3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3)", which looks like weeks rather than people, and the ghost fifth cell is not explained, so I need a second look.
screens.why_b3: It is recognisably my quoting rhythm, but "get approval for an enterprise deal quote" narrows what I typed ("a buyer has asked for a quote and the pricing has to be worked out and approved") to its approval step.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic; it does not say that one more countable answer would settle it, or that the four counted all lean my way.
screens.why_b5: It refuses to call four people, says outright "a small group: a lean, not a call", and names Connor and Mei-Ling and why they were not counted, so nothing is overstated.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 6 counted, and all 4 approve quotes in 2 to 4 of the last 4 weeks (middle 3); one more countable answer would settle it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted with 5 needed, and the So line repeats both, so I know why nothing is called.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count 8 picks from 4 people, but the strip under them reads 'for 3, against 5', which mixes picks with people; I had to look twice to see that the bar's '3 of 4' means 3 of my 4 reps, with only Mateo against.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Importance and its belief line is word for word what I checked: quoting is one of the two things my account executives most want made easier.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' tells me to wait, but it never says the plain next step: one more counted rep would decide it, and right now 3 of 4 is leaning my way.
screens.why_b5: Nothing is overclaimed and the low count is called a lean, but the verdict says '4 answered' while the count line says '6 answered', and 'against 5' on the strip could read as five reps against me.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 reps who could be counted put quoting in their two, which is above your 2 in 3, but one more counted answer is needed to call it; Mateo, whose CPQ already quotes, was the one against.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats '4 counted, 5 needed'.
screens.why_b2: The chart clearly counts how my last-quote pricing went, but three different numbers sit close together: 6 answered, 4 counted, and five strip cells including a ghost. The label 'your bar · 3 of 4' also reads as either the bar or the tally until I work out that 2 in 3 of 4 means 3.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Current solution and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, Sheets, slides, CRM entries and email chains included.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say I am one counted answer short, or that the lean already runs my way with 3 of 4 falling short.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and flagged as 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and 3 of 4 at the bar is not dressed up as a held belief, so nothing overreaches.
screens.instead: Leaning your way: 3 of the 4 counted (Jordan, Priyanka, Aisha) fell short, but that is one short of the 5 needed to call it; get one more account executive to answer about their last quote.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Too few to call', with '4 answered · 5 needed to call it' right under it, so I know there is no verdict yet and the number that explains why.
screens.why_b3: The Importance name and my belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in, though the Current solution belief I also checked gets no box and no note.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next: there is no line telling me to get one more answer or what to change, and no hint about whether a CPQ already doing the quote matters for my pitch.
screens.why_b5: The n stays plain ('1 against · 1 asked their why here', 'On their own (1)'), the low count is called too few, and one rep's answer is not passed off as a pattern.
screens.why_b6: Mateo's answer gives me something I did not write: a rep whose price book is already in the CPQ quotes in minutes and spends the week on pipeline and forecast, so CPQ users are a segment where my pain may not be the top one.
screens.instead: Too few to call (4 of 5): one rep with a CPQ said quotes take minutes and pipeline and forecast matter more. Get one more answer, and ask whether your reps already have a CPQ; also show why Current solution has no box.

screens.why1: As the opening screen it checks whether I've had a recent enterprise quote to talk about, which is the obvious place to start.
screens.why2: Getting a quote approved is everyday language for me as an AE and I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I price and quote enterprise deals and chase the approvals myself, so I know whether one went through in the last month.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate should carry no escape, and here there are two chips; 'I'd rather not say' is not an allowed escape, and 'I can't recall one particular quote' reads oddly on a simple yes-or-no.
screens.why5: Asking whether I 'got approval' drifts slightly from pricing a deal that has to be worked out and approved, because a quote still stuck in the approval wait, or one turned down, would push me toward No even though it is exactly the situation the study is about.
screens.why6: Spoken, it is one short question followed by 'Yes or no,' which is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 4 weeks, did you price an enterprise deal quote that needed sign-off? Yes · No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: I just said yes to getting a quote approved in the last month, so asking how often comes naturally next.
screens.why2: "In how many weeks did you get approval" is clumsy; I had to read it twice, because I think in deals and quotes, not in weeks that had an approval.
screens.why3: I know which deals I got signed off, but turning that into a count of weeks means flipping through my calendar and guessing a bit.
screens.why4: One to four covers it after the yes, the numbers don't overlap, and "I can't recall" is the honest way out.
screens.why5: It's about getting a quote approved, which is my world, and nothing about anyone's product slips in.
screens.why6: Short and one question, but "in how many weeks did you get approval" is a mouthful to hear once before "a number from 1 to 4" lands.
screens.instead: How many of the last 4 weeks did you get a deal quote approved? 1, 2, 3 or 4 -- or I can't recall.

screens.why1: After I've picked what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last quote actually went with the tools I use is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I know every tool named, but 'your last quote' then 'each deal' makes me reread: was it one quote or all of them, and nobody prices a deal 'in slides'.
screens.why3: I build and chase approval on my own quotes in sheets, CRM and email every week, so I can answer straight from the last one.
screens.why4: Each option bundles how I priced with how approval went, the first two both mean 'quick and clean', and the usual case is missing: built it fine, then waited two days on approval.
screens.why5: The question takes the founder's list of Sheets, slides, CRM and email as given for how I price, and 'guessed a discount' sounds like a judgement on reps rather than my words.
screens.why6: A twenty-word stem with a four-tool list, then five comma-split two-part options, is a lot to hold heard once.
screens.instead: Think of your last enterprise quote. How did getting it priced and approved go? Done the same day; built quickly, then waited days on approval; had to rebuild the numbers to get it approved; went back and forth over email on terms; or say I can't recall.
